content.text: Chapter Three
The Returning Exiles
The summons came while Falanaras was still sweating from drills.

The training yard behind the garrison barracks was white stone and packed dirt, hemmed by scaffolding where masons were resetting a fallen cornice. Spellbreakers ran forms in pairs, blades turning in short, hard arcs, shields lifting to catch the morning light. Falanaras worked the second rank with a borrowed glaive that was too long for him, his shoulders aching, his breath sharp. Every few minutes a magister’s apprentice passed along the line with a floating crystal, green-lit and humming, and men stepped aside to breathe from it, to let the ache behind the eyes ease.
“At ease,” the master-at-arms called. “Courtyard duty. Dress ranks.”
Falanaras lowered the glaive. Theron beside him rolled his shoulder and muttered, “We’ve not done courtyard duty in weeks.”

“The city’s receiving guests,” Lethira said from the end of the line. She had been watching the gate street. “High elves. By sea,” she added, quieter. “Two ships put in south of the city. They came up the coast road on foot.”
No one answered at first. The word itself had become unfamiliar in Silvermoon, a name that belonged to letters and memory.

They washed, belted on clean tabards — the new red, darker than blood, stitched with the phoenix — and formed at the Shepherd’s Gate, where the road from Eversong entered the inner city. The wind came down the Dead Scar and carried dust that never quite settled. The gate’s guards had polished their armor. Behind them, fel crystals set in braziers burned low and steady along the wall, their light catching in every eye that passed, turning the green there a little brighter.

Silvermoon had learned to look presentable around its wounds. Banners hung straight. Children were kept back from the road. Magisters stood in threes, hands folded, observing. Falanaras took his place with the second rank and felt the familiar pull behind his teeth, the thin restlessness that came before the hour he usually fed. He stared at the crystal in its brazier and then forced his gaze back to the road.
Most came on foot, as if to show they meant no threat.

There were perhaps twenty of them, with two rangers riding as outriders and a train of two wagons behind. The first thing Falanaras saw was the color. Blue. The pale, clear blue of the old Alliance tabard and the silver-white of cloaks kept clean despite the road. The high elves walked with the weary, upright bearing of travelers at the end of a long journey, their faces thin. At their head rode a woman with silver hair bound back, a ranger’s bow across her back, and the posture of someone accustomed to being looked to.
Vereesa Windrunner.

The name moved down the line in a whisper. Even the magisters straightened. For a heartbeat the yard forgot the fel light and the hunger and remembered what it had been to hear that name beside Sylvanas and Alleria, when the Windrunners had been a living wall around the kingdom.

Behind her, a little to the left, walked a man in a simple blue cloak over a travel-worn doublet. His hair was the red-gold of House Dawnspear, cut shorter than Falanaras remembered. He had his mother’s narrow jaw. He walked with his hands empty at his sides, as if he did not know what to do with them.
Falanaras’ grip tightened on the glaive without his telling it to.
Caelir.

His older brother had been in Dalaran when the Scourge came, studying under the Kirin Tor. The last letter had come long before the fall — more than a year and a half old now, ink smudged, full of lectures and a promise to write again at winter’s end — and it said nothing of war or survival, because no war had yet reached him. After Silvermoon fell there had been no more letters at all. Falanaras had written his name twice into the lists of the missing kept at the city registry and had stopped only when Theron told him to stop counting the dead twice.

Caelir was looking at the gate, at the crystals, at the phoenix banners snapping red over white stone. His eyes found the brazier nearest Falanaras and stayed there. The green reflected in his own eyes — his eyes were still blue, clear, untouched — and his mouth thinned.

The column halted. Vereesa dismounted. Lor’themar Theron waited under the arch with Ranger-General Halduron Brightwing and a small escort, his cloak plain, his missing eye hidden in shadow. Lor’themar stepped forward and gave the measured bow of a ruler receiving an honored commander.
“Lady Windrunner,” Lor’themar said. His voice carried without shouting. “Quel’Thalas welcomes you home.”

Vereesa bowed her head. “Lord Regent. We came as soon as we could. Word reached us late, and the roads out of Dalaran have not been kind.” Her Common was crisp; her Thalassian accented the way the diaspora’s Thalassian always was, a little careful. “We brought medicines, linen, some grain. It is not much.”
“It is not small to us,” Lor’themar said. “You will be housed as kin. Enter.”

The guards stepped aside. The high elves passed through the gate, and the line of spellbreakers had to make an aisle for them. Falanaras stood shoulder to shoulder with Theron, eyes forward, and felt Caelir come nearer step by step. The smell of travel — horse, wool, pine soap unlike the perfumed oils used in Silvermoon now — reached him.
Caelir stopped directly before him. The line could not accommodate a private meeting, but no officer ordered them on.
“Falanaras?” Caelir said, quiet.
Falanaras swallowed. “Caelir.”

His brother looked older than Falanaras remembered: lean from months of poor sleep, his Dalaran beard kept short. His gaze dropped to the glaive, the tabard, the bracer on Falanaras’s forearm, then returned to his face.
Caelir lifted a hand as if to touch his shoulder and checked himself. “You’re alive,” he said. His voice broke on the second word, and he forced it steady. “When the ravens stopped, we — I thought —”
“I’m alive,” Falanaras said. It sounded blunt. He tried again. “You are. I did not know.”

Behind Caelir, the rest of the exiles kept moving, but a few had slowed to watch. A woman with dark hair — one of the Dalaran survivors, by her robes — stared at the fel brazier with undisguised alarm. A younger high elf stared at Falanaras’ eyes and then quickly away.

Caelir noticed. His frown settled on the brazier itself, on the way the rank had placed it where every soldier on duty would breathe it regularly. “What is that?” he asked, too softly for the officers to hear.
“A crystal,” Falanaras said. “For steadiness.”
“It is fel,” Caelir said. It was not a question.
Falanaras did not flinch. He had learned not to. “It is what we have.”

Caelir’s jaw worked. He looked past Falanaras to the city beyond the gate — the scaffolds, the red banners, the thin figures moving in the streets with the quick, efficient steps of people who kept near sources of power. “We heard things in Dalaran,” he said. “That you were — that the city had turned to drawing on — we did not believe it was like this. So open.”
“We do not hide it,” Falanaras said. “Hiding does not help.”
The master-at-arms’ voice cut in, low and firm. “Dawnspear. Let your brother pass inside. You will have leave at evening.”
Falanaras nodded once. Caelir’s hand finally found his forearm, squeezed, and let go. The touch was brief and hot.
“Evening,” Caelir repeated.
“Evening,” Falanaras said.
The exiles continued into the courtyard. Falanaras watched his brother’s cloak move with the others until the gate’s shadow cut it, and the ache behind his eyes came back, louder now.
Leave came at the sixth bell.

Falanaras changed out of the tabard and went to the pilgrim house by the eastern market where the exiles had been quartered. The building had been a clothier’s shop before the Scourge; its upper floor still smelled of cedar and old dye.
Caelir was waiting in the doorway, as if he had been listening for footsteps. He had washed, but he wore the same blue cloak.
“You came,” he said.
“I said I would.”

They stood there a moment too long. Then Caelir stepped forward and embraced him. It was tight and awkward, shoulder to shoulder with no armor between them, and Falanaras felt how thin his brother had become under the cloak, and how quickly his own throat closed.
“You’re taller,” Caelir said into his shoulder, trying to laugh. He pulled back and looked at him. “Or I remember you shorter.”
“You remember correctly. I grew after you left.”

Inside, the pilgrim house’s common room had been cleared for the guests. Bowls of soup steamed on a long table, and a fel crystal in a simple iron stand burned on the mantel, as every mantel in Silvermoon now held one. Its light was low, tended by a matron who kept the house. The high elves sat around it without seeming to know they had leaned away.
A woman — the dark-haired one from the gate — glanced at the crystal and then at Falanaras, and colored. “We are grateful for the lodging,” she said carefully in Thalassian.
“It is bare,” Falanaras said. He did not move the crystal. To move it would have been to make a statement of its own.
Caelir gestured to a bench near the window. “Sit. Tell me —” He stopped, overwhelmed by the size of the question. “Tell me everything. Father — did he —”

“Father is dead,” Falanaras said. He had learned to say it plainly, because hesitation made it worse. “I found him in the house before I fled the western quarter. When the Scourge withdrew, I went back and buried him.”
Caelir closed his eyes. For a long moment his breathing was the only sound. When he opened them they were wet. “And you were alone?”
“Not alone. I was with the retreat through the east gate. Theron — you would not know him — and others. After, I took service. It was the only way to stay.”

Caelir nodded, as if service were natural. He was trying to fit the facts into the brother he had known, the boy who had sulked over calligraphy and loved hawks. “You wear the phoenix now,” he said. “The red.”
“We are sin’dorei,” Falanaras said. The word came easily now, with practice.
Caelir flinched. “Don’t.”
Falanaras looked at him. “It is what we call ourselves.”

“You were quel’dorei when I left,” Caelir said, his voice low. “We were quel’dorei. The name was given for suffering, yes — I understand that. But the change — Fal, do you know what you look like to those who have not been here? Your eyes —” He gestured, helplessly. “The crystals in every house. The way your soldiers breathe them in like air. In Dalaran we heard rumors. Mana-tapping. Keeping live — creatures — for feeding. We thought it was Alliance slander. Vereesa said we should see for ourselves before we judged.”
“And now you have seen,” Falanaras said.
Caelir’s hands were shaking. He clasped them. “I hardly recognize our people,” he said. “Forgive me. I mean no insult to your survival. I cannot understand this as survival. This is alteration.”

The matron came by with a tray. She offered Caelir a small, cut crystal on a porcelain dish, the way one would offer a sweet after a meal. “For the chill, sir,” she murmured. “The house keeps them for guests who feel the draft.”
Caelir stared at the dish. “No,” he said, too loud. “No thank you.”

The matron’s smile stiffened. She offered the dish to Falanaras. He took a shard out of habit, let its faint warmth touch his palm, then set it back. “Thank you,” he said to her. She left, her jaw tight.
“You see?” Caelir said when she was gone. “You offer it as courtesy. You do not see how it looks.”
“I see,” Falanaras said. “I live here.”

The room had gone quiet. Other high elves were listening without staring. Falanaras felt the heat rise in his neck, the old defensiveness that came whenever someone who had not been in the city judged it.

Caelir leaned forward, earnest. “Come back with us. Or come to Dalaran, at least. There are magisters among us studying the hunger. We share what stores remain and use disciplines that ease the withdrawal. You would not need to —”
“Without what?” Falanaras asked. “Without living here?”
“Without fel,” Caelir whispered.

Falanaras looked at the crystal on the mantel. It burned steady and green, and in its light the room’s white stone seemed less white. He thought of Murder Row at night, of the Wretched he had helped drag from a cellar last week, jaw slack, eyes blind with craving. He thought of the way his own hands steadied after a controlled draw, and how shameful it was to need that steadiness.
“You should see more of the city before you ask me that,” he said at last. “Walk with me tomorrow. I ask only that you see.”
Caelir searched his face. “Will you show me the house?”
The western quarter. Falanaras had not been there since he had buried his father. “Yes,” he said.

They sat a little longer, trying to talk of smaller things — hawks, tutors, whether old Master Aldris still kept his terrible toupee — and failing. When Falanaras left, Caelir walked him to the door and gripped his arm once more, hard.
“I missed you,” Caelir said. “Every day.”
Falanaras nodded, because his throat would not let anything else out.
Outside, the night air was cooler. Theron was waiting across the street, out of sight of the pilgrim house windows, arms crossed.
“Well?” Theron asked.
Falanaras fell into step beside him. “He’s my brother.”
“And?”
“And he thinks we have poisoned ourselves to live,” Falanaras said. He could still feel the grip on his arm. “He is not entirely wrong.”
Theron was quiet a street longer. “Tomorrow will be worse. They are to be received in the court. Vereesa will speak.”

Morning came pale over the eastern sea. Falanaras met Caelir at the courtyard fountain where the water ran thin over repaired stone. Caelir had slept poorly; the skin beneath his eyes was shadowed. He carried no gifts, no parchment — only himself, as if any offering would have been presumptuous.
“You said you would show me,” Caelir said.

They walked west. Silvermoon woke around them in its careful way. Shop shutters lifted. A baker set out loaves that were smaller than Falanaras remembered from childhood but evenly divided. Apprentices moved in pairs to check the crystals set at street corners, tapping each with a wand, noting the resonance in small books. Where the light burned steady, people lingered a moment longer before moving on; where it sputtered, they touched their temples, frowned, and walked faster.

Caelir watched it all without comment at first. His horror had settled into something quieter, more attentive. At the colonnaded arcade, a magister was teaching children how to breathe — in through the nose, out slow, hands hovering near a crystal without touching it, as if learning to sip rather than gulp. One boy’s hands trembled until the magister steadied them.
“You teach them young,” Caelir said softly.

“We must,” Falanaras said. “Untaught hunger makes Wretched. You remember the stories from the outskirts. Murder Row has earned its name. Last month three of them broke into a cellar looking for an old mana cache and tore one another apart before the guard arrived. We keep the young close to steady sources so they learn measure.”
Caelir’s mouth tightened. “In Dalaran they call it dependency. They study it as a malady.”

“It is a malady,” Falanaras said. “And it is also life. We call it hunger because craving is only part of it. The emptiness after the Sunwell reaches beyond the blood. We do not speak of it often because speaking changes nothing. We offer a crystal, we move nearer a ward, we keep working. What would you have us say?”

They had reached the edge of the ruined quarter. The street ended where the Scourge had ended it. Beyond a temporary wooden barrier, the western district lay open to the sky, its white stone blackened, its towers broken like teeth. The barrier was guarded, though no one lived there and few wished to enter. Wind moved through the empty shells and lifted ash that had never quite washed away.

Falanaras stopped at the line where the cobbles gave way to scorched earth. “House Dawnspear stood there,” he said, pointing to a plot now marked only by a low foundation and a singed tree that had somehow survived. “Two floors, a courtyard with a lily pool. Our father kept his books on the second. He died inside. The Scourge left many houses in this quarter with no bodies to bury.”
Caelir stepped past the barrier before Falanaras could warn him. He knelt at the foundation and set his palm on the stone. His shoulders rose once, hard.

“I was in Dalaran when the sky broke,” Caelir said, his voice rough. “We felt the wind from the north. The masters said Quel’Thalas had fallen. I told myself you might have fled east, that you were clever enough to run. I told myself many things while I was safe behind another city’s walls.”
Falanaras joined him on the other side of the barrier. The ash was fine and clung to their boots. “You were not safe. Dalaran fell too, later. I heard.”

“It did. I survived again, by luck and by being moved to the outer vaults when Antonidas ordered the evacuation. That is my history since I left — survival by being elsewhere.” Caelir looked up, eyes red. “Do you understand why I cannot hear that name without grief? Sin’dorei. You rename yourselves for the dead while you —” He gestured back toward the crystals, the city, the green light. “While you make yourselves unlike them.”

“We rename ourselves because we are unlike them now,” Falanaras said. “Quel’dorei is what we were when the Sunwell lived. That people is gone. The name matters because it tells the truth. We are blood elves. Blood for what was lost. It is in their honor.”

“The name matters,” Caelir repeated, and for a moment they agreed without knowing it. Then he shook his head. “But truth should not be purchased this way. I saw your soldiers, Fal. Their eyes. I saw the way that matron offered fel as if it were tea. You have let Rommath and his green fire into every house. It will mark your children.”

“Our children will live,” Falanaras said. The words came sharper than he intended. He steadied himself. “You were not here when the hunger took hold. You did not see elders weep because they could not remember a spell, or a boy of nine scratch his arms raw in the night. Rommath brought us a way to keep the ache from eating us alive. The means are dangerous. So is every choice left to us. The wards hold. The Scourge have not returned through the Scar this winter. That is what living looks like here.”
Caelir stood, brushing ash from his knees. “And Kael’thas? Is he the one who approves it? From wherever he is, chasing salvation in Outland?”

Falanaras felt a flicker of the old hope, stubborn even after disappointment. “He named us. He went to find help. Lor’themar holds the city in his name. Grand Magister Rommath speaks for him. We believe he will return with something better than crystals. Until then we hold.”
“Faith in a distant prince,” Caelir said, not unkindly. “It is a thin rope to hang a kingdom from.”
“It is a rope nonetheless,” Falanaras said.

They walked back slowly. Near the bazaar, a patrol passed with a man in custody, his eyes too bright, his wrists bound in cloth to keep him from clawing. The high elves’ escort tightened around Vereesa’s people when they saw it, while the blood elves on the street barely turned their heads. They had seen it too often. Caelir stared until the patrol turned the corner.
At noon the city gathered.

The Court of the Sun still bore the Scourge’s damage: half its colonnade scaffolded, its far wall patched with timber. Lor’themar had ordered it opened for the exiles. Blood elves filled the tiers in quiet ranks: magisters in red-trimmed robes, Farstriders with bows unstrung, matrons with children kept close, veterans with empty sleeves. Falanaras stood with his unit near the base of the dais, Theron and Lethira on either side. On the dais itself, Lor’themar waited with Halduron and Rommath, the latter’s presence a statement in itself, his robes immaculate, his eyes lit faintly green.

Vereesa entered with her company. She wore no crown, no high jewelry, only the battered silver of a ranger who had ridden far. Yet the hall quieted as if a queen had entered. She stopped before the dais and bowed.

“People of Quel’Thalas,” she said, and her voice carried. She spoke in Thalassian, clear and unadorned. “We left as high elves. We return and find you calling yourselves sin’dorei. We do not come to quarrel over a name. We come because we heard that you live, and we could not stay away.”
A murmur ran through the tiers, soft, involuntary — welcome and warning at once.

Vereesa continued. “In Dalaran we mourned you. We kept your scrolls, your songs, your heraldry behind our walls. We defended your name when others said Quel’Thalas was ended. When the Kirin Tor turned their minds to new dangers, some of us argued that aid should be sent sooner, faster. We were not heeded as we wished. For that, I ask your forgiveness.”
She paused, and her gaze lifted to the crystals burning on the pillars, to the green wash over the crowd, to Rommath’s still face.

“Grief cannot govern sight,” she said, quieter now. “What we have seen in your streets troubles us. The fel you burn openly. The hunger you feed with power taken by force from living things — and I have been told you teach your children to draw it. In exile we learned to endure the same ache differently. It is hard and slow. We did not smother it with demon fire. We fear for you as kin, afraid that the means you have chosen will leave you unable to be who you were, even if the Sunwell were restored tomorrow.”
The hall was utterly still. Falanaras felt Theron’s hand brush his forearm, a warning to keep his face blank.

Lor’themar stepped forward. He did not raise his voice. “Lady Windrunner speaks as one who loves Quel’Thalas, and we honor it. No one here will pretend our condition is wholesome. Neither Grand Magister Rommath nor I. Dalaran had protected stores and allied lands able to sustain you. We had the Scar at our door and winter coming. Our people stood in the ash of their houses and shook until they could not hold a cup. We chose a hard sustenance over a slow fading. Judge the choice. Remember the place where it was made.”

Rommath’s smile was thin. “Your exiles endured beyond our borders, Lady Windrunner. Here, endurance required invention. The crystals you dislike are warded, measured, and distributed. Without them the Wretched would number in hundreds more. You speak of what we might be if the Sunwell returned. We speak of whether any of us will live until then.”
Vereesa did not look away. “And the tapping? The draining of others to sate yourselves? Is that invention also measured?”

A hiss went through the magisters. Lethira, beside Falanaras, exhaled through her teeth. Falanaras kept his eyes on Vereesa, and for a moment the symbol gave way to a ranger who had walked too many burned villages, whose bluntness was grief made strict.

“Mana-tapping sustains many,” Rommath said evenly. “It is governed, and no one is compelled while other sources suffice. Restraint and meditation have their uses. They do not feed every child or hold a single ward.”

Vereesa bowed her head again, accepting that no agreement would be reached there. “Then I ask only this. Do not close the road between us. Let letters pass. Let those who wish to live as quel’dorei be welcomed when they seek you, and let those who wish to remain sin’dorei be known for their endurance rather than their excess. The Alliance is not your enemy if you do not make it so.”

Rommath’s mouth thinned. “The Alliance you speak for did not seem so even-handed when Grand Marshal Garithos caged our prince in Dalaran and condemned his soldiers to death for accepting naga aid. Forgive us if we learned there that Alliance friendship is conditional upon our obedience — and our disappearance.”

Lor’themar answered for the city. “The road will remain open to our kin. You will have quarters here, and escort where the Ghostlands allow.” It was courteous and final. The court clapped, relieved that the confrontation had stopped short of rupture. The applause held little fervor.
After, the hall emptied slowly. Falanaras looked for Caelir in the dispersing crowd and found him near a pillar, alone, his face pale with the effort of holding his tongue through Vereesa’s speech.
“You heard her,” Caelir said when Falanaras reached him. “She was restrained, and even so they took it as accusation.”
“She told the truth as she sees it,” Falanaras said. “And Rommath told ours.”

Caelir stepped closer, lowering his voice so only his brother would hear. “Stay quel’dorei with me. I am asking for your sake alone. You do not need to call that light beautiful to survive it. Come to Dalaran for a season. See that hunger can be borne without fel. If it cannot, you can return. I will not hold it against you.”

The offer was sincere, and that made it harder to refuse. Falanaras thought of the pilgrim house, of the crystal offered like a sweet, of the way his own hands had steadied after a draw. He thought of the foundation in the ash and the phoenix on his tabard.

“I am sin’dorei,” he said. It was a boundary now. “I did not choose it to spite you. I chose it because I stayed. You stayed elsewhere and kept the old name honorably. That is your path. Do not ask me to walk it as if I had not buried anyone.”
Caelir’s eyes filled. “The name matters,” he said again, and this time it sounded like a plea. “If you change what you are called, you change what you will permit yourself.”
“Then perhaps you do not know me,” Falanaras whispered. The words escaped before he could soften them. Caelir flinched as if struck.

Caelir recovered, his jaw set in the familiar Dawnspear stubbornness they had shared as boys. “I will not report to Dalaran that you are lost,” he said. “Only that you are — changed. And that you would not come.”
“Report that I am alive,” Falanaras said. “And that House Dawnspear still has a son in Silvermoon who remembers his brother.”
They embraced once more, brief and hard, as they had at the gate. This time neither tried to laugh.

The exiles left two days later, as they had come — on foot to the coast, with wagons lighter now for having left their stores. Silvermoon did not polish itself for their departure. Only the daily watch lined the road. Falanaras stood in the second rank without his glaive, his hands empty at his sides. Vereesa rode at the head, her face forward. Caelir walked near the middle of the column. He did not look for his brother until the very end, when the road bent south toward the harbor. He turned then, found Falanaras, and lifted a hand. Falanaras lifted his in return. The distance was already too great to read the other’s eyes.
The column passed out of sight. The wind came down the Dead Scar again and lifted dust over the white stone.
That evening, Falanaras went to the barracks’ small shrine — no priestess served there now, only a basin and a phoenix etched in the wall — and stood a while before report. Theron found him there.
“You did not yield,” Theron said.
“Neither did he,” Falanaras said.
“Will you write to him?”
“Yes,” Falanaras said. “When I know what to say that will not be a lie.”

Above the city, the fel crystals lit one by one as dusk fell, green against the rose of evening, steady and unhidden. From the barracks wall, Falanaras could see the dark reach of the western quarter where his brother would never now live. The hunger moved through him in its slow, familiar pull. Beside it lay the fresher pain of a living brother lost to another name, another loyalty. Both would have to be borne.
